clue.text: Home counties, whatever their speed, have the marine spirit

blocks.note: the Home Counties surround London in the south-east of England, abbreviated SE
any speed at all is 'any mph', miles per hour

explanation.surface: Commuters from the counties around London, fast or slow, share some salty seafaring spirit.
explanation.walkthrough: The Home Counties are the counties around London; they lie in the south-east, SE. Read 'whatever their speed' as ANY MPH and the answer is SEA NYMPH.
explanation.definitionFit: A sea nymph is a minor goddess of Greek myth living in the ocean, so a spirit of the marine world.

clue.text: Agree to stop moving

blocks.note: first meaning: come to terms, as in a dispute agreed out of court
second meaning: come to rest, as dust or a bird does

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as agreeing to a ceasefire; the two halves are separate senses of one verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To settle a dispute is to reach terms, and to settle is also to come to rest and stay still.

clue.text: You could say a nose-rag was a necessity for the Greeks

indicators.note: what you could say is what is spoken, so the sound of the words counts, not their spelling

blocks.note: a nose-rag is a hanky, a handkerchief; say it with the h dropped

explanation.surface: A cheeky claim that the ancient Greeks could not do without a handkerchief.
explanation.walkthrough: Drop the h, cockney-style, from 'a hanky' and it runs together as ANANKE.
explanation.definitionFit: Ananke is the Greek personification of necessity, compulsion and inevitable fate, worshipped as a primordial goddess.

clue.text: 11 gold sovereigns leased, with exterior locks

indicators.note: something on the exterior sits outside, so these letters wrap round all that came before

blocks.note: Yale is a well-known brand of door lock
OR is gold in heraldry
K for king, twice over for the plural
leased means rented, hired out

explanation.surface: A rental agreement paid in gold coins, with the premises secured by locks.
explanation.walkthrough: Sovereigns looks like the gold coins but means kings, abbreviated K. 11 is the down entry NATIONAL PARK, so this is one of Britain's national parks.
explanation.definitionFit: The Yorkshire Dales in northern England is one of the national parks of England and Wales, designated in 1954.

clue.text: 11 requiring obedience after vegetable upset kid

indicators.note: upset means knocked over and disordered, so the letters of the next word are rearranged

blocks.note: a pea is a small green vegetable
the letters of kid, jumbled
a strict parent or teacher requires obedience

explanation.surface: A disciplinarian parent insisting a sulky child behaves, after an upset over eating greens.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after' places the requiring-obedience word last. 11 is NATIONAL PARK; the Peak District in Derbyshire was Britain's first.
explanation.definitionFit: The Peak District, in the hills of Derbyshire, was the first national park designated in Britain, in 1951.

clue.text: See 18
Home for bird or fairy, say?

indicators.note: say asks for the word as spoken, so it must match by sound only

blocks.note: fairy-like, delicate and ethereal is airy, as in airy-fairy

explanation.surface: Asking whether a nest belongs to a bird or to a fairy.
explanation.walkthrough: EYRIE has two accepted pronunciations, one of which rhymes with 'fairy' and sounds just like AIRY, light and insubstantial.
explanation.definitionFit: An eyrie is the high nest of an eagle or other bird of prey, so a bird's home.

clue.text: French food in the East containing a load

indicators.note: containing means holding something within, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: est is the French word for east, in keeping with the French theme
a cargo is a load carried by a ship or plane

explanation.surface: A French dish travelling in a shipment to the Orient.
explanation.walkthrough: The French word EST, east, holds CARGO: ES-CARGO-T.
explanation.definitionFit: Escargots are edible snails, a classic dish of French cuisine served with garlic butter.

clue.text: According to Lent's use, rendered without melody

indicators.note: rendered means performed in a new version, so the letters are given a different arrangement

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Lenten church music, performed in the austere manner the season demands, without any tune.
explanation.definitionFit: Tuneless describes singing or music that lacks a tune, so it has no melody at all.

clue.text: Interval to find bear lost in wood

indicators.note: something lost has gone astray, so the letters wander into a new order
in places one piece inside another

blocks.note: the letters of bear, rearranged
teak is a hard tropical wood

explanation.surface: A break taken to search for a bear that has wandered off in the forest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Interval' suggests music or theatre, but here it is a pause at work.
explanation.definitionFit: A tea break is a short pause in work for a drink, an interval in the working day.

clue.text: 11 is here and here again with king replaced by aces in different places

blocks.note: surface reading: a national park found in one place and found again somewhere else

blocks.clueFragment: with king replaced by aces in different places
blocks.note: setter's reading: take the town, swap its R (rex, king) for two letters A and S placed in separate spots, and you get BEACONS, the rest of the park's name

explanation.surface: A puzzling directory entry for a park that seems to be in two places at once.
explanation.walkthrough: The park, the Brecon Beacons, is named after this Welsh town. Remove R from the town, put A in the middle and S at the end, and the town becomes BEACONS.
explanation.definitionFit: The Brecon Beacons national park in south Wales takes its name from this market town, so the park is literally here.

clue.text: Race to put your car here!

definitions.text: Race to put your car here!

blocks.note: the Grand National is Britain's famous steeplechase, called simply the National
to park is to put your car somewhere and leave it

explanation.surface: An exclamation urging drivers to hurry to a car park, or a racecourse.
explanation.walkthrough: The Grand National is the steeplechase at Aintree near Liverpool. The whole clue also hints at the answer: a big area of countryside you drive to and park in.
explanation.definitionFit: A national park is a protected area of countryside visited by motorists, and it is the theme linking many other entries.

clue.text: 11 shows king amid returning security

indicators.note: amid means in the middle of, so one piece sits inside the other
returning means going back the way it came, so the word is read from right to left

blocks.note: a seal secures a document or container
K is the abbreviation for king in chess

explanation.surface: A national park shows its king surrounded by guards on his way home.
explanation.walkthrough: K goes inside SEAL (SE-K-AL), then the whole is read backwards. 11 is NATIONAL PARK: the Lake District, often just the Lakes.
explanation.definitionFit: The Lakes is the everyday short name for the Lake District national park in Cumbria, north-west England.

clue.text: Girl back later, possibly, crossing the circle

indicators.note: back means the word is read backwards
possibly suggests one of several arrangements, so the letters may be reordered

blocks.note: a maid is a girl, here read backwards
the letters of later, rearranged

explanation.surface: A girl may come back later, perhaps crossing a ring on her way.
explanation.definitionFit: Diametral means relating to a diameter, the straight line passing through the centre of a circle from side to side.

clue.text: Footwear from American football?

blocks.note: in the US the football is nicknamed the pigskin, after the leather it was once made from
shoes are everyday footwear

explanation.surface: A shopper asking what kind of shoes a gridiron player wears.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition and the wordplay at once: footwear made from the material of an American football. The question mark flags the playful reading.
explanation.definitionFit: Pigskin is leather made from pig hide, used for gloves and shoes as well as the American football.

clue.text: 11 turned down when held by Mrs Gandhi

indicators.note: turned means twisted round into another shape, so the letters are rearranged
something held by another is gripped inside it

blocks.note: Sonia Gandhi, widow of Rajiv and leader of India's Congress Party
the letters of down, rearranged

explanation.surface: A national park refused by Mrs Gandhi when it was offered to her.
explanation.walkthrough: S(NOWD)ONIA. 'Mrs Gandhi' suggests Indira, but by 1999 Sonia was the one in the news. 11 is NATIONAL PARK; Snowdonia is in north Wales.
explanation.definitionFit: Snowdonia, the mountainous region around Snowdon in north Wales, was designated a national park in 1951.

clue.text: Rider*s cape has the same turned in

indicators.note: turned means twisted into another shape, so the letters are rearranged
has means holds within, so one piece goes inside another
in confirms the jumbled piece sits inside

blocks.note: Cape Horn, the southern tip of South America, is often simply the Horn
the letters of same, rearranged

explanation.surface: A rider's cape has had its matching lining turned inside.
explanation.walkthrough: The asterisk stands for an apostrophe: 'Rider's' is 'Rider is'. HOR(SEMA)N puts the jumbled letters inside HORN.
explanation.definitionFit: A horseman is a man who rides horses, so a rider, especially a skilled one.

clue.text: The flag is nothing special

blocks.note: first meaning: a banner, especially a regimental or royal one
second meaning: ordinary, of the usual kind

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as a shrug about a dull flag; the two parts are different senses of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: A royal or regimental banner is called a standard, and standard as an adjective means ordinary, the normal model.

clue.text: Awfully kind offer to go in where Bobby may be almost finished?

indicators.note: awfully means very badly done, so the letters are scrambled
to go in means placed inside something else

blocks.note: a bobby is a British police officer, who walks on the beat, a patrol route
the letters of kind offer, rearranged

explanation.surface: A very generous proposal to enter a place where a policeman might be standing.
explanation.walkthrough: The jumbled letters go inside ON THE BEAT after ON THE B. 'Awfully kind' reads as very kind, but awfully is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Being on the brink of defeat means close to losing, so the struggle is nearly over and lost.

clue.text: 11 used to play Othello?

blocks.note: ex- means former, one who used to be something
Othello is Shakespeare's Moor of Venice, so an actor playing him is a Moor

explanation.surface: A national park that once played Shakespeare's Moor on stage.
explanation.walkthrough: An actor who used to play Othello is an ex-Moor. 11 is NATIONAL PARK: Exmoor straddles Somerset and Devon in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: Exmoor is moorland in Somerset and Devon that was designated one of the national parks of England in 1954.

clue.text: Models remodelled once in a blue moon?

indicators.note: remodelled means given a new shape, so the letters of the word before are rearranged

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Fashion models getting a makeover, which happens only rarely.
explanation.definitionFit: Once in a blue moon is an idiom for very rarely, which is what seldom means.

clue.text: Songs about detectives on return from soviet-style government

definitions.note: the answer is an adjective describing this kind of government

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one piece goes round another
on return means coming back, so the whole is read from right to left

blocks.note: a lay is a song or ballad
the CID is the Criminal Investigation Department, the British police detective branch
taken as written

explanation.surface: Songs about police detectives who have come back from a Soviet-run regime.
explanation.walkthrough: LA(CID ON)YS read backwards. A soviet is literally a council, and a synod is a church council, so 'soviet-style' fits.
explanation.definitionFit: Synodical describes rule by a synod, an elected council, just as a soviet was a governing council.

clue.text: See 3
Confederacy on fire?

blocks.note: first meaning: the southern states of the US that formed the Confederacy
second meaning: an army cooking pot, which goes on the fire

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as the South burning in the Civil War; the second sense is the dixie, a large iron cooking pot or camp kettle used by soldiers.
explanation.definitionFit: Dixie is the nickname for the American South, and a dixie is a military cooking pot set over a fire.

clue.text: Spotted snake's head in prude's mouth?

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter
in places one piece inside another

blocks.note: a prim person who avoids speaking plainly is mealy-mouthed
the first letter of snake

explanation.surface: A spotty snake's head ends up in the mouth of a prim and proper person.
explanation.walkthrough: MEA(S)LY. The question mark admits the stretch: a prude's mouth is a mealy mouth.
explanation.definitionFit: Measly literally means having measles, the disease that covers the skin in red spots.

clue.text: It is not by way of encroachment following mother

indicators.note: following means coming after, so the encroachment word is placed second, behind the word for mother

blocks.note: ma is an informal word for mother
an inroad is an advance into someone else's territory

explanation.surface: A legal point that something is not done by way of trespass, after Mother complains.
explanation.walkthrough: 'following mother' puts MA first. 'by way' must be read as 'byway', a minor side road.
explanation.definitionFit: A main road is a major route, the opposite of a byway, which is a small back lane.

clue.text: Would-be stripper causes hell among teachers

indicators.note: among means in the midst of, so one piece sits inside another

blocks.note: the NUT was the National Union of Teachers, a British trade union
Dis is the classical underworld, hell

explanation.surface: A wannabe striptease artist causes uproar in the staff room.
explanation.walkthrough: NU(DIS)T. Dis is the Roman god of the underworld and, in Dante, the city of hell.
explanation.definitionFit: A nudist likes to go naked, so is someone keen to strip off all their clothes.

clue.text: X-ray to remove top from around Indian city

indicators.note: around means surrounding, so one piece wraps the other

blocks.note: to skim milk is to remove the cream from its top
Agra is the Indian city of the Taj Mahal

explanation.surface: An X-ray used to peel back the roof of a city in India.
explanation.walkthrough: SKI(AGRA)M.
explanation.definitionFit: A skiagram is an old term for a radiograph, a shadow picture produced by X-rays.
